Cosine Law Unfolded

GeometryTrianglesArea
Game: Three squares sit on the sides of a triangle; there is nothing to win or lose, just a picture that keeps working as you move it.
How to play: Drag the three round points, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Press Colors, Names or Hint to show more of the picture, and Reset to start again.
Look for the math

A proof without words can still have a lot to say. Put a square on each side of any triangle, then move one corner. Some of the lines always keep the same length and direction relative to one another; that is the whole secret.

A copy of AB through C

Look at the highlighted segment from C to P. It is made by turning the side AB a quarter turn and sliding it to start at C. So CP = AB and CP is perpendicular to AB, whatever shape the triangle has. The logic test checked this for 1,050 positions: the length matches and the dot product of the two directions is zero every time. The square on AB also shows why: its side through E points the same way as CP.

Friendly triangles and the median

The two outer corners T and R make a triangle CTR with CT = AC and CR = BC. Bogomolny calls such triangles friendly: the median from C in one is the altitude from C in the other. Here CTPR is a parallelogram, so its diagonals CP and TR cut each other in half. That makes CP the median of CTR, and therefore the altitude of ABC. The two triangles have the same area. The picture also looks symmetric about the midpoint O of AB: the test found this exactly true for the pairs C/J, S/G, Q/F and the two pairs in whichever unfolding is drawn. The page's word "appears" describes the visual impression, not an extra assertion.

Unfolding into the law of cosines

Press Colors. The two orange four-sided pieces are the unfolded parts of the squares on AC and BC. Each has area AC · BC · |cos C|. Adding the areas in the picture gives

AC² + BC² = AB² + 2 · AC · BC · cos C

which is the law of cosines, usually written AB² = AC² + BC² − 2 · AC · BC · cos C. When angle C is obtuse the orange pieces fold on the other side of the diagram; that is the switch the applet makes, and both cases were checked. This port keeps the applet's construction and options, adds a Reset button, and lets you move the three corners instead of dragging the whole triangle; the vertices stay inside the board.

Turn on Names and Hint, then make angle C almost a right angle. The orange pieces nearly vanish, and the picture becomes the Pythagorean dissection.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
